items.title: investigating, debugging and solving memory leaks in javascript and react
items.summary: The first time I saw it, I did not know what I was looking at. I had DevTools open on an app I was building, and the memory graph kept climbing like a staircase. Up, flat, up, flat, never really coming back down. The app felt fine for the first five minutes. After twenty, everything was sluggish. That staircase is the universal sign. Something in my code was holding onto memory it should have let go of. JavaScript cleans up after you. When nothing references an object anymore, the garbage collector frees it. A memory leak is when something you forgot about keeps a reference alive, so the collector can never do its job. It is not dramatic. There is no error, no crash, at least not at first. Just a slow climb until the tab gets heavy and your users start complaining that the app "feels slow lately". In every leak I have ever tracked down, the culprit was one of these. No exotic stuff, just boring mistakes: Event listeners with no cleanup. You add one in a useEffect, the component unmounts, the listener stays. Mount it ten times, you have ten listeners. items.title: Your unsubscribe link works. Gmail still won't show 'Unsubscribe'. Here's what's missing
items.summary: Your marketing emails have an unsubscribe link in the footer. You've clicked it. It works. Your sending dashboard still warns about "missing one-click unsubscribe", and Gmail never shows the little Unsubscribe button next to your sender name. That's because the link in your footer and "one-click unsubscribe" are two different things. Since 2024, Gmail and Yahoo have required bulk senders to support one-click unsubscribe as defined in RFC 8058: two specific email headers plus an endpoint that unsubscribes someone with a single POST, no login, no confirmation page and no "are you sure?". If any of those pieces is missing or slightly wrong, mailbox providers treat your email as not having it. This post walks through the full implementation: the headers, the endpoint (and why it must ignore GET), signed tokens, DKIM coverage, and how to test it with curl. There are three parts, and you need all three: A List-Unsubscribe header containing an https URL for this recipient. A List-Unsubscribe-Post header with the exact value List-Unsubscribe=One-Click. items.title: Streaming JSONL in Node.js still needs a record limit
items.summary: A file can be streamed and still contain a record too large to hold in memory. For JSONL processing, the useful bound is the size of the largest record you are willing to decode, as well as the stream's chunk size. This matters for log exporters, data imports and transcript readers. A missing newline or a giant embedded tool result can turn an otherwise ordinary file into one enormous record. readline is late Node's readline interface emits a complete line when it reaches a line ending, or when the input ends without a final line ending. By the time a consumer checks line.length, that line has already become a JavaScript string. A stream's highWaterMark is a buffering threshold. It does not establish a maximum application-level record size. The stream documentation also distinguishes a threshold from a strict memory limit. For a JSONL reader with a hard record limit, frame records in bytes first. Once the current record crosses the limit, discard its fragments until the next newline. Decode only records that stayed within the limit. Save this as bounded-lines.mjs. It splits on LF bytes, which also works for JSONL files using CRLF because the remaining carriage return is valid JSON

Its biggest strength is that it feels close to plain HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, so you can read a Vue file and understand what it does without learning a whole new way of thinking first. How does Vue work? A Vue component is a single file with three parts: a template that looks like HTML, a script block with your JavaScript, and a style block with your CSS. When your data changes, Vue updates only the parts of the page that need to change. You do not write code to find elements and update them by hand — you describe what the page should look like for a given state, and Vue keeps the page in sync. That idea is called reactivity, and it is the core of Vue. Vue is a good fit for beginners because it grows with you. You can start by adding Vue to a single HTML page with a script tag and making one button interactive. Day 45 — WEB + BACKEND ENGINEERING Authentication is the process of verifying who a user is before allowing access to protected resources. Let's take a Flutter application with a Node.js/Express backend. When a user logs in, here's what happens: The Flutter app sends login credentials to the backend over HTTPS. The backend validates the input. It checks the user's credentials against securely stored password hashes. If the credentials are valid, the backend issues an access token. Flutter securely stores the token and uses it for protected API requests. Example: POST /api/auth/login After successful authentication, the backend may return: { "accessToken": "your-access-token", "expiresIn": 900 } For protected endpoints, Flutter sends: Authorization: Bearer The backend verifies the token before processing the request. It comes down to three operational realities: how tightly your product needs to couple with device hardware, your organization's engineering topology, and your capital efficiency timeline. For most business applications, customer portals, and transaction workflows, React Native unifies product velocity across platforms while preserving native interface fidelity. Pure native development remains the right call when your app is essentially an extension of device hardware or requires uncompromising platform specialization. items.title: Skip weekends and holidays in scheduling with a holidays API
items.summary: Scheduling can be a complex task, especially when you need to exclude weekends and holidays from your calculations. No setup, no library of pre-made caches to manage — you just open the app and play the hunt that is right in front of you. items.summary: Introduction In today's digital world, software applications and online services may experience unexpected failures, errors, and performance issues. Identifying the root cause of these incidents quickly is important for maintaining reliable services. To address this challenge, I developed IncidentMind – an AI-Powered Incident Analysis and Management System. IncidentMind is designed to help users analyze incidents, understand possible causes, and generate recommendations for resolving technical problems through an easy-to-use dashboard. Problem Statement When an application experiences an unexpected failure, developers and support teams need to understand: What went wrong? What might be the root cause? How serious is the issue? What actions should be taken to resolve it? How can similar incidents be prevented in the future? Manually analyzing incidents can take time. IncidentMind aims to make this process more organized and efficient. Project Overview The application includes a dashboard for incident analysis and sections for viewing past incidents, analytics, and settings. items.title: How are you dealing with all the negative side effects of AI on the web?
items.summary: It seems to me that the AI hype killed the web for good, but not for the reasons we immediately associate with it. Search engines now rank links full of slop at the top, which ironically make LLM summaries acceptable, not because they are better than what we had before (they are not), but because they at least mention the good links which are now buried at the bottom of the page. Also, they've been rate limiting ordinary users like crazy: more often than I'd like to, Google and DuckDuckGo now either show me either an error message or tell me to wait a bit. Sometimes I waste at least a minute refreshing the page and waiting for a result. I also can't browse GitHub freely without being logged in. Anubis is now everywhere, occasionally blocking me. I feel like my productivity has actually gone down thanks to all of that. Edit: I see that most of the replies here are suggesting relying less on the web and going after more fundamental resources, which are great suggestions, don’t get me wrong! items.title: I Built an AI Support Agent That Never Repeats a Failed Fix Using Hindsight
items.summary: ResolveIQ is a support workflow built around that distinction. It combines ordinary operational records in PostgreSQL, a language model for drafting replies, and Hindsight for customer-level memory across conversations. The through-line is simple: a proposed fix is not a resolution. We need to know what was tried, whether it worked, and what the next response should avoid. A support agent can sound attentive while making a customer repeat the same troubleshooting step for the third time. I wanted the system to remember the outcome, not just the conversation—and to make that memory useful on the next ticket. The application has a React and TypeScript frontend, a FastAPI backend, and PostgreSQL records for customers, tickets, conversations, messages, resolution attempts, and escalations. The support agent uses a server-side Groq client to generate a response. Hindsight provides retain, recall, and reflect operations for customer memories. I keep those responsibilities separate. PostgreSQL owns facts that need explicit structure and predictable updates: the ticket state, the assignment, the message history, and each attempted solution’s outcome. items.title: I Parsed the Same Format String Five Million Times
items.summary: I had an exporter writing CSV lines, one per row, millions of rows a night. Nothing clever in it: a string.Format call with a template and three values. It was slower than it should've been, so I put a profiler on it, and the call that lit up wasn't the file write or the decimal math. It was the formatting. Specifically, it was the part of string.Format that reads the template "{0},{1:yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss},{2:F2}" and figures out where the holes are. That work was happening on every single call, and my template never changed. When you call string.Format(format, args), the runtime has to walk that format string, find the {0}, {1:...}, {2:...} placeholders, pull out the alignment and the format specifiers, and only then start stitching the output together. That parsing step is pure overhead if the template is a constant, which it almost always is. You wrote the template once in your source code. The runtime rediscovers its structure five million times. CompositeFormat is the fix, and it's about as simple as it gets. You parse the template once into a CompositeFormat object, then hand that object to string.Format instead of the raw string. items.title: A New JsonSerializerOptions Every Call Cost Me 120x
items.summary: A list endpoint on one of my services started showing up heavier in the traces than it had any right to be. It pulled a small object, serialized it, returned it. The payload was tiny — an order with three line items. But under load the thing allocated like it was streaming a video, and the CPU time didn't match the shape of the work. I went looking for the expensive query. There wasn't one. The expensive part was the return. Here's the line I'd written, more or less, inside the handler: var json = JsonSerializer.Serialize(order, new JsonSerializerOptions { PropertyNamingPolicy = JsonNamingPolicy.CamelCase, DefaultIgnoreCondition = JsonIgnoreCondition.WhenWritingNull, Converters = { new JsonStringEnumConverter() }, }); Looks fine. It is not fine. That new JsonSerializerOptions { ... } sitting inside a method that runs on every request is the whole bug. I used to think JsonSerializerOptions was a settings bag — a few flags, a naming policy, done. It isn't. items.title: Vibrating Mattress Helps Clear Alzheimer's Protein From the Brain
items.summary: A vibrating mattress combined with two pills that release nitric oxide enhanced the brain's ability to clear an Alzheimer's-related protein. According to New Scientist, the experiment "caused the brain's blood vessels to swell and constrict more strongly, which enhanced the glymphatic system's clearance of [the protein]." From the report: [Kesa Kiviniemi at the University of Oulu in Finland] and his colleagues recruited 29 adults who hadn't been diagnosed with Alzheimer's disease or any other cognitive issues. The participants took a pill that dissolves when under the tongue, releasing nitric oxide. They then lay on a mattress that caused their bodies to gently vibrate for 40 minutes, taking another pill halfway through. Blood samples revealed that their levels of a type of protein called beta-amyloid 42 increased by 35 per cent, on average, after the intervention. This protein, which usually helps neurons signal and connect to each other, misfolds and form clumps in Alzheimer's disease. items.summary: Acts of greyzone aggression aim to spread panic. Europe has to show the saboteurs that we are resilient It was as though a ghostly hand had switched the settings on supermarket freezers across Europe from “freeze” to “defrost”. From Finland to Ireland, they suddenly began heating up, many reaching 50C and food worth millions of euros had to be thrown away. But no actual hand was needed to cause the meltdown. This was a cyber-attack, or rather a chain of attacks. Like pretty much everything else in 2026, supermarket freezers are digitally enabled. That makes them smarter and more efficient, but like everything else that is connected to the internet, it also makes them more vulnerable. Russian hacktivists claimed they were behind some of the supermarket sabotage, but no one knows for sure. It could also be Iran, Iranian proxies, North Korea – or unaffiliated bedroom hackers. [This policy has to be published permanently on their website and in their terms of service, and it must include a basic way to notify users. In other words, what can be terminated is the Internet connection itself, not just an account. According to Mexican business outlet EL CEO, this means that access providers such as Telmex and Izzi will need such a policy.] The Senate approved the amendments with roughly two-thirds of the vote, as the opposition voted against. The Chamber of Deputies already approved the same text in October, so the decree now goes to President Claudia Sheinbaum. Her government proposed the changes in May to bring the law in line with the USMCA trade agreement between Mexico, the United States and Canada. items.title: Day 14: Extension Points on a Business Object and When to Override Them
items.summary: Behavior a definition can express needs no code written at all. The ones it cannot express are what needs taking over: what to check before this document is submitted, who to notify after it is saved, and under what circumstances a delete is not allowed. The way the framework offers to take over is inheriting from a business object and overriding a few of its steps. A subclass adds this form's own logic at the matching step as required, and the hard part is judging which step is the matching one, and whether that code belongs before or after base. A method name can only answer the order, with DoBeforeSave before the save and DoAfterSave after it. The rest has to be stated by the framework. items.title: EU Says TikTok's 'Rabbit Hole' Effect Must Stop
items.summary: The European Commission has preliminarily found that TikTok violates the Digital Services Act because its For You recommendation algorithm can create a "rabbit hole effect," repeatedly exposing users to potentially harmful content involving topics such as sadness, isolation and body image. TikTok must change the feed's design or potentially face fines of up to 6% of its global annual revenue. The Verge reports: The findings come months after the EU Commission declared that TikTok's design is too "addictive." While TikTok has implemented controls to mitigate the algorithm's "rabbit hole effect," the Commission says its preliminary findings suggest that they're not effective. TikTok must now change the design of its For You feed, or else face fines of up to 6 percent of its global annual turnover. The platform is also facing pressure in the US, with lawmakers and a wave of lawsuits raising concerns about child safety. items.title: How I built a Wordle-style daily puzzle in SwiftUI (no backend)
items.summary: I recently shipped Gemdoku: Daily Block Puzzle, a 9×9 block puzzle for iPhone. The core feature is a Wordle-style Daily Challenge: every player in the world gets the same goal, the same move limit and the exact same sequence of pieces each day. It turned out to be a fun little engineering problem. Here's how it works under the hood, all in plain Swift and SwiftUI, with no backend. The obvious way to give everyone the same puzzle is to generate it on a server. I didn't want a backend. The game is fully offline, has no accounts and collects no data. So the daily puzzle has to be derived, not downloaded. The trick is a seeded random number generator. Swift's RandomNumberGenerator protocol makes this easy. items.summary: Roku is removing its popular Aquatic Life fish tank screensaver on December 1 and automatically switching affected users to Roku City. According to Cord Cutters News, the creator pulled the license after Roku's sale to FOX was announced. Ars Technica reports: The screensaver has been an option for Roku OS users for 10 years. Roku has been licensing the animation, which is called the Marine Aquarium, from artist Jim Sachs through Prolific Publishing. Sachs is the creator and copyright holder of the Marine Aquarium. He developed the screensaver through his company SereneScreen. He tells Ars Technica that the licensing agreement with Roku is up for renewal every October and can be canceled by either party for any reason. A day after learning that Fox was planning to buy Roku, a deal that closed today, Sachs told Prolific that he wouldn't be renewing Roku's license. "I can't be part of the Fox world," he tells Ars, pointing to Fox News' controversial style of news and entertainment. Roku will automatically switch the Aquatic Life screensaver on affected devices to the Roku City screensaver, another popular animation that includes subtle advertisements, according to the user notice. items.title: Hangfire Alternative in .NET: Why I Replaced It With BackgroundService and Channel
items.summary: The first version of this site was an ASP.NET Core MVC app with Hangfire wired in: a dashboard at /hangfire, five recurring jobs, ten places in the code that called BackgroundJob.Enqueue, and a second SQL Server database just to hold Hangfire's job tables. When I rewrote the backend as a separate Web API, I didn't bring Hangfire with me. The API that serves this page runs two BackgroundService classes fed by System.Threading.Channels, and one WHERE clause does the work of the every-minute job. This isn't a "Hangfire is bad" post. Hangfire is a good library. It's a post about checking which jobs actually needed it, because for this site the answer was none of them. The short version: Use Hangfire (or Quartz.NET) when a job must survive a restart, retry on its own, or be visible on a dashboard. If the work is in-process, short-lived and fine to lose on a crash, a BackgroundService with a bounded Channel is built into .NET, needs no extra database, and is about 60 lines. A job that only "flips something on at a certain time" often needs no job at all: filter by time in the query. items.title: Britain to Make Salary Disclosure In Job Ads Mandatory
items.summary: Britain plans to require employers to disclose salaries in job advertisements. "Whether you're a young person starting out or a parent trying to support your family, you should know what a job pays before spending your time and effort applying for it," Prime Minister Andy Burnham said in a statement. Reuters reports: The government said requiring companies to disclose pay in job ads would help young people applying for their first jobs, while boosting pay transparency and helping tackle disparities that can disadvantage women. Just over two in five employers always publish salary ranges, while fewer than one in five always disclose specific salaries, Burnham's office said, citing estimates from the Chartered Institute of Personnel and Development. The government will soon introduce legislation to parliament making salary disclosures mandatory, Burnham's office said, although it did not provide a timeline. Nearly one million, or 13%, of 16 to 24 year-olds in Britain are not in employment, education or training, one of the highest shares in Europe. A government review into youth inactivity is due to be published later in November. Read more of this story at Slashdot.

items.title: When “Working as Designed” Is the Problem
items.summary: I submitted a security report to Anthropic after Claude Code exposed my .NET User Secrets in its model context. They classified it as “Informative – Working as Designed.” “Working as designed” is a triage label, not a verdict. But taken at face value, it points to something architectural: security is enforced tool by tool, not around the agent as a whole, and certainly not at the OS-boundary level. .NET developers commonly use dotnet user-secrets to keep development credentials in their user profile, outside the project tree. These secrets can include: • API keys • Database connection strings • Passwords • Third-party service credentials • Other sensitive application configuration Consider this scenario: You have a .NET application. You have configured User Secrets. You launch Claude Code in your project directory. You ask Claude to inspect your application configuration. Claude can execute: dotnet user-secrets list And/or read the plaintext secrets.json file. %APPDATA%\Microsoft\UserSecrets\ \secrets.json Because tool output is returned to Claude, those credentials become part of the conversation context. items.title: Permission-heavy multi-tenant systems: make the access check boring
items.summary: Permission-heavy systems become risky when access rules are scattered across controllers, UI checks, repository filters, and background jobs. The aim is not a clever authorization framework. It is one rule path that is difficult to bypass. The examples come from Shield, Zotic, CAS, Question Banking and Amlaak. Every protected operation can be described with four values: the actor, the tenant, the action, and the resource. If one is unknown, the system does not yet have enough information to allow the operation. This simple tuple prevents a common mistake: checking that a user has a permission somewhere, then loading a resource that belongs to another tenant. Permission and ownership need to be evaluated together. The decision input public sealed record AccessRequest( Guid ActorId, Guid TenantId, string Action, string ResourceType, Guid? items.title: They Created a Cell That's Almost Alive. What to Do With It Now? (8 minute read)
items.summary: A SpudCell is an artificial cell created from lifeless ingredients that can grow, copy its DNA, divide in two, and start its cell cycle all over again. It is still far from a self-sustaining cell that any scientist could manufacture from prepared ingredients, but the technology could eventually make it easier to produce medicines, foods, and other items that could not otherwise be produced with ordinary biology. The researchers working on SpudCell hope that it will eventually be a platform for biotechnology that will allow a simple cell to be engineered in scores of useful ways. SpudCell could potentially be misused, so its researchers are taking security seriously from the start - its DNA and proteins are engineered so that it can only survive on an exotic diet of chemicals not found in nature.

items.title: Mining 14,351 Chess Puzzles with Stockfish 18 (and the Illegal-FEN Trap in chess.js)
items.summary: When we started building Brass Pawn (source on GitHub, AGPLv3), we needed a large offline tactics, positional judgement, and endgame dataset that ran completely on-device—both in the browser and natively on iPhone, iPad, and Mac. Transcribing chess puzzles by hand or scraping unverified problem collections breaks down fast. Two failure modes show up immediately in real training: Cooked solutions: A position has a flashy sacrifice, so a human annotator marks it as winning—missing a quiet defensive resource at depth 18, or missing a second equally winning move that punishes a student for playing an objectively strong alternative. Horizon flips: A shallow engine pass (depth 10–12) flags a move as +2.10, only for depth 22 to reveal perpetual check (0.00). Instead of transcribing puzzles, we built a deterministic mining and independent verification pipeline powered by Stockfish 18. Along the way, we hit a subtle FEN validation edge case in chess.js that silently breaks UCI engines. A good tactics puzzle isn't simply "someone blundered in a game." items.title: Making a SwiftUI app survive a folding iPhone: what broke on the iPhone Duo and how I fixed it
items.summary: I make PawLife, a small pet health app (feeding plans in grams, a health diary, a food safety lookup). It is one SwiftUI codebase for iPhone, iPad, Mac Catalyst, Apple Watch and visionOS. When Xcode 27.2 shipped simulators for the iPhone Duo, I expected "it is just a wider iPhone". It is not. Here is what actually broke, in the order I found it, and what the fixes looked like. The Duo has an outer display and an inner one across the fold. Your app runs on one of them at a time, and the window changes size when the user folds or unfolds. The simulator reports it as a window resize, not a new scene. Measured on the simulator: Folded: a 466×678 pt window, of which my app got 382 pt of width. The remaining 84 pt on the trailing edge is a reserved column (status area and camera) exposed through the safe area. Open: a landscape 951×669 pt window, 867 pt for the app, with the same 84 pt trailing column. So the app goes from a narrow portrait phone to a wide landscape slab and back, live, without a relaunch. items.title: iOS silent push not working: content-available and background pushes
items.summary: A silent push, which Apple calls a background notification, has no alert, sound or badge. It wakes your app so it can fetch new content. Apple treats it as low priority and does not guarantee delivery, so "it worked once and then stopped" is often the system working as designed. This page goes through what must be right on the sender and in the app, and what the device itself decides. What you see Likely cause Fix Never arrives, alert pushes work Remote notifications background mode not ticked Signing and Capabilities > Background Modes > Remote notification Shows a banner instead of waking the app quietly alert, sound or badge in aps next to content-available Send aps with content-available: 1 and nothing else APNs returns 400 apns-priority: 10 with apns-push-type: background Priority 5 for background pushes, always Delivered late, or in bursts Priority 5 pushes are sent according to the device's power state Expected; use an alert push for anything a person waits for Arrives in testing, then stops Throttled: too many background pushes Two or three an hour at most Nothing after the user swiped the app away The app was force quit Nothing to fix; it wakes again once the user opens it

items.title: Understanding SwiftUI's layoutPriority: HStack, ZStack, and Custom Layouts
items.summary: SwiftUI makes building interfaces straightforward, but its layout system can sometimes produce unexpected results. One modifier that developers often reach for is .layoutPriority(). For example: swift This can help resolve layout issues, but what exactly does the priority value mean? And does the modifier behave the same way in every container? To explore these questions, I built an interactive open-source project called SwiftUI Layout Lab. The .layoutPriority() modifier provides a priority value that parent layouts can use when determining how to size their children. The default priority is 0. A higher priority doesn't directly specify a width, height, or percentage of available space. Its effect depends on the parent layout algorithm and the sizing behavior of the child views. For example, assigning a priority of 100 doesn't mean a view will receive 100 times more space than a view with priority 1. An HStack arranges views horizontally, but what happens when there isn't enough space for every view to receive its preferred width? In Layout Lab, you can: Select one of three views. Change its layout priority. Adjust the available container width. Observe the actual measured widths.

items.title: Crop Once, Post Everywhere: Batch Aspect-Ratio Crops for Social Images in Swift
items.summary: If you ship photos from an iPhone app to more than one place, you eventually hit the same boring problem: Instagram wants 1:1 or 4:5, a shop banner wants 16:9, Stories want 9:16, and the camera roll is full of 4:3 and 3:4 stills. Doing that crop by hand for thirty product shots is how afternoons disappear. This post walks through a small UIKit pipeline that takes one UIImage, a list of target aspect ratios, and returns one centre-weighted crop per ratio — suitable for running across a whole album. I’m writing it from the seat of someone who builds BatchMark, an on-device batch photo app, where “apply the same finishing step to many photos” is the whole product. The code below is a teaching extract, not a dump of the app. People say “crop to 1:1” and mean two different things: Aspect-fill crop: keep the photo’s resolution as high as possible, cut off the edges that don’t fit the ratio. Aspect-fit pad: show the whole photo, add bars (or a mat) to reach the ratio. For social uploads you almost always want (1). items.title: The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time review – a dream come true
items.summary: Nintendo Switch 2; Nintendo This ambitious remake transforms a landmark Zelda game into a modern masterpiece, clearer and easier to navigate, more beautiful to look at, with playful musical touches. Yet the melancholy remains It’s always a worry, returning to a formative piece of art from your childhood. Will your jaded adult sensibilities render you unable to locate the magic that captivated your child self? Will revisiting it reveal that it was never actually that good, and that your tastes are built on a foundation of lies? With video games, there is the added complication of technological advancement: decades-old games can look so basic and feel so treacly to play that it’s hard to explain why they were mind-blowing at the time. Light-touch remasters aim to bring such games up to modern graphical standards without fundamentally changing them; an ambitious remake attempts to transform the work into something that can stand alongside any modern masterpiece. items.title: ‘There is no inevitable dystopia’: Jeanette Winterson on AI and the future of humanity
items.summary: The author believes we are at a turning point as a species – and even in the shadow of big tech it’s up to us how we want to proceed ‘I am a storyteller by trade,” writes Jeanette Winterson on the first page of her 2021 book 12 Bytes, an idiosyncratic and thought-provoking series of essays in which she considered just how artificial intelligence might change everything about our lives. “And I know everything we do is a fiction until it’s a fact: the dream of flying, the dream of space travel, the dream of speaking to someone instantly, across time and space, the dream of not dying – or of returning.” She had already been thinking about our possible futures for at least 15 years – her 2007 novel, The Stone Gods, for instance, imagined a post-climate catastrophe world populated by robots and humans who never age, while 12 Bytes was preceded by Frankisstein: A Love Story, which alternates a recreation of the summer Mary Shelley wrote Frankenstein with a trans doctor’s travels among present-day cryogenecists and AI-enabled robots. items.title: The sleep framework: A new way for LLMs to retain knowledge in continual learning (11 minute read)
items.summary: Researchers have developed a new way to enable large language models to integrate new facts and enhance reasoning without catastrophic forgetting or static knowledge cutoffs. Alternating between active interaction and offline memory consolidation allows LLMs to continuously acquire new facts, retain long-context knowledge up to 10M tokens, and improve complex reasoning.

items.summary: The Audacity is a fearless satire taking on Silicon Valley’s ‘egomaniac weirdos’. Its creator and stars talk ayahuasca ceremonies, mining kids for data – and punching CEOs Showrunner Jonathan Glatzer wanted the tagline of his latest TV creation to be: “We’re so fucked.” He laughs. “Sadly it got rejected by the network. Hey, maybe I can use it for season two!” The show in question is The Audacity, his darkly comic drama about AI tech titans.
